title: Henry Ford: The Good, Bad and Ugly
summary: Josh and Chuck (with iHeart Intro voice) profile Henry Ford: his birth and childhood in Dearborn, Michigan, early car ventures (Quadricycle, Detroit Motor Company, Henry Ford Company, racing to win Alexander Malcolmson's backing), founding of Ford Motor Company in 1903, the Model T and Model A, the assembly line, the $5 workday and the Sociological Department, his personal life (wife Clara, alleged affair with Evangeline Coat, son Edsel's troubled relationship with him and Edsel's death in 1943), his anti-Semitism and the Dearborn Independent and The International Jew, his pacifism and the Peace Ship, his libel suit against the Chicago Tribune, his buyout of the company, River Rouge plant, Greenfield Village, Harry Bennett and the Battle of the Overpass, and his death in April 1947. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about a mysterious 1980s song.

segments.title: Opening banter and casting jokes
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode with light banter, joking about who should play Henry Ford in a biopic and noting his plain appearance.

segments.title: Early life and first car experiments
segments.summary: Ford's birth in Dearborn, Michigan in 1863, his parents, his one-room schoolhouse education, his interest in engines, marriage to Clara, work with Thomas Edison, and early horse-riding accidents that spurred his interest in machinery.

segments.title: Quadricycle and early car companies
segments.summary: Ford built the Quadricycle, gained investor William Mayberry's backing, and formed the Detroit Motor Company in 1899, followed by the Henry Ford Company, which failed; the latter became Cadillac. Ford then raced cars to attract investors, leading to Alexander Malcolmson.

segments.title: Founding Ford Motor Company and early models
segments.summary: Ford Motor Company was founded in 1903 with Malcolmson's help. The Model A sold in 1903-1905 era and a series of letter-designated models followed, including the luxury B and K models and cheaper C, F and N-type buggies.

segments.title: Ouster of Malcolmson
segments.summary: Malcolmson pushed for luxury cars while Ford wanted affordable ones; Ford had Malcolmson pushed out of the company in 1906.

segments.title: Model T, affordability, and the assembly line
segments.summary: The Model T launched in 1908 at about $850, reshaping car ownership. Production grew rapidly. The hosts explain that Ford did not invent the car or the assembly line but combined conveyor-based assembly in a new way, which led to high worker turnover and falling prices.

segments.title: The five-dollar workday
segments.summary: Ford introduced a five-dollar workday, which was publicized as profit sharing and reduced turnover, while the hosts note this image was not entirely accurate.

segments.title: Ford Sociological Department
segments.summary: The Sociological Department made home visits to check workers' habits such as drinking and boarding; the hosts discuss how Ford controlled workers through company housing.

segments.title: Affair with Evangeline Coat
segments.summary: Ford married Clara and had a long-standing affair with Evangeline Coat, who married his associate Ray Dollinger; Ford reportedly had a son, John, with her, and built a secret staircase to her bedroom.

segments.title: Edsel Ford and father-son conflict
segments.summary: Ford's son Edsel was treated harshly by his father, who undermined him, including ordering an office wing foundation left unfilled. Edsel died in 1943 at age 49, reportedly from stomach cancer or a raw milk reaction; Ford blamed the doctors.

segments.title: 1919 Dodge lawsuit and stock buyout
segments.summary: Ford lost a lawsuit requiring dividend payouts to the Dodge Brothers, then announced he would leave, prompting stockholders to sell shares to an investment company Ford controlled, giving him, his son and wife outright ownership of Ford Motor Company.

segments.title: Pacifism, World War One and the Chicago Tribune libel suit
segments.summary: Ford was a pacifist who spoke against World War One and chartered the Peace Ship; he backed the war once America entered. He was later interviewed by the Chicago Tribune, sued for libel after an editorial, won six cents, and was exposed as ignorant on the stand.

segments.title: Dearborn Independent and anti-Semitic publications
segments.summary: Ford bought the Dearborn Independent in 1919 and ran articles claiming Jewish control of finance and other ills, compiled into The International Jew, which was distributed widely. Ford was sued for libel by Aaron Sapiro and settled with a public apology.

segments.title: Ford's ties to Hitler
segments.summary: Ford's admiration for Hitler is discussed: Hitler cited Ford as an inspiration and displayed his portrait, and Ford accepted an award from Hitler in 1938.

segments.title: River Rouge Plant and Model A revival
segments.summary: The River Rouge Plant, a vertically integrated 2,000-acre complex opening around 1918, made Ford dominant. Sales declined in the mid-1920s, leading to the Model A in 1927.

segments.title: Greenfield Village and nostalgia
segments.summary: Ford built Greenfield Village, a living history village modeled on his childhood, including a one-room schoolhouse and dance instruction, and moved Menlo Park buildings there, while his company was run by Edsel, Charles Sorenson and Harry Bennett.

segments.title: Harry Bennett and the Battle of the Overpass
segments.summary: Harry Bennett's Ford Service Department opposed unionization; in 1937 the Battle of the Overpass saw union organizers and reporters beaten, which damaged Ford's reputation and helped the UAW organize; Ford workers later voted to unionize.

segments.title: Ford's final years and death
segments.summary: Ford's health and memory declined, he opposed FDR and the New Deal, Edsel's death and Ford's brief return as president, his retirement in 1945, and his death on April 7, 1947, after an aneurysm.

segments.title: Closing banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke about Ford's death and the Italian impression, then transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail about mysterious song
segments.summary: Listener Nicole from Germany shares observations on an earlier episode about a mysterious 1980s song, suggesting East German origin and a possible smuggled broadcast. The hosts thank her and give the email address.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Standard iHeartRadio sign-off.
